summary: Specifies a DHCPv4 option that tells a host the network supports IPv6-only operation and lets the host forgo obtaining an IPv4 address if IPv6 connectivity is provided. It also updates RFC 2563 on DHCP server behavior for certain requests. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A network can say to a device: "you don't need the old kind of address here, the new kind is enough." This document defines how the network says that, which can save old addresses for those who still need them.

questions: what is the ipv6-only preferred dhcpv4 option
how does a host skip ipv4 on an ipv6-only network
how does a host skip ipv4 with dhcp
subtitle: A DHCPv4 option that lets IPv6-capable hosts skip IPv4 addresses when the network says IPv6 alone is enough.

tldr.problem: Networks that mix IPv6-only-capable hosts with hosts that still need IPv4 usually split them into separate segments, which is complex and error-prone. A host also cannot tell in advance whether a network offers IPv6-only service.
tldr.mechanism: A capable client lists option code 108 in its DHCPv4 Parameter Request List. A server on an IPv6-mostly pool answers with the option, whose value is a wait time in seconds, and the client then stops DHCPv4 for that time instead of taking an IPv4 address.
tldr.outcome: IPv6-only, dual-stack and IPv4-only hosts can share one segment, and IPv4 is turned off only when both client and server agree. The RFC also updates RFC 2563 so that servers still answer such clients.

today: RFC 8925 is a Proposed Standard from October 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 2563.

sections.title: Why IPv6-Only Needs a Signal
sections.content:
Some hosts can run on an IPv6-only network, either because everything on them supports IPv6 or because they use a translator such as 464XLAT. Others still need an IPv4 address. Operators who want to roll out IPv6-only incrementally have traditionally put the two groups on separate network segments or Wi-Fi SSIDs. The RFC lists the drawbacks: more segments mean operational complexity and higher memory use for access control list entries, and hosts can end up on the wrong segment (for example, the user picks the wrong SSID).

Just turning IPv4 off on capable hosts does not work, because those hosts must still function on IPv4-only networks. A host also does not know what kind of network it has joined, so it normally starts configuring IPv4 and IPv6 at once. Waiting for IPv6 to be confirmed would slow down IPv4-only and dual-stack networks, and releasing an IPv4 address after applications have started using it could cause visible errors.

The RFC's answer is a new DHCPv4 option through which a client says that IPv4 is optional for it, and the network says that IPv6-only service (NAT64, with DNS64) is available. The goal is an IPv6-mostly segment, where IPv6-only, dual-stack and IPv4-only hosts coexist.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a school where some kids need a paper pass and others do not. Instead of two separate doors, the guard asks each kid and only hands passes to those who need one.

sections.title: Why DHCPv4 Carries the Signal
sections.content:
The RFC argues that DHCPv4 is the natural place for this signal, since it is already the protocol used to configure IPv4 on hosts. It gives three reasons.

  • Letting a network remotely disable IPv4 on a host could be seen as a new denial-of-service vector. Using DHCPv4 limits the attack surface to DHCPv4-related attacks without adding new vulnerable elements.
  • IPv4 is disabled only if both the client and the server indicate IPv6-only capability. Otherwise the host works in dual-stack or IPv4-only mode, and it gets an address as quickly as any other host.
  • DHCPv4 is client/server, so IPv4 can be switched off per host on a segment. That preserves scarce IPv4 addresses and simplifies incremental deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The address desk already talks to every device when it arrives, so it is the easiest place to add one more question. Nothing changes unless both sides say yes.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The IPv6-Only Preferred option has a code, a length and a value. The code is 108, assigned by IANA. The length excludes the code and length fields; the server MUST set it to 4, and a client MUST ignore the option if the length is anything else.

The value is a 32-bit unsigned integer: the number of seconds for which the client should disable DHCPv4, known as V6ONLY_WAIT. If the server pool is explicitly configured with a V6ONLY_WAIT timer, the server MUST put that value in the field. Otherwise it MUST set the field to zero.

The client never sends the full option. It only lists code 108 in its Parameter Request List.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a tiny note with a label, a size and one number. The number says how many seconds the device should wait before asking again.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 client SHOULD let an administrator mark IPv6-only capability for one interface or for all interfaces. A client on an IPv4-requiring host MUST NOT include the option code in its Parameter Request List and MUST ignore the option if a server sends it. A client on an IPv6-only-capable host SHOULD include code 108 in the Parameter Request List of DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages.

If the DHCPOFFER carries a valid option, the client SHOULD NOT request the offered IPv4 address. It sets the V6ONLY_WAIT timer to the received value, or to MIN_V6ONLY_WAIT if the received value is smaller, and SHOULD stop DHCPv4 configuration for that many seconds or until a network attachment event, whichever comes first. The host MAY disable its IPv4 stack on that interface for the same period. It MAY also configure an IPv4 link-local address.

If a DHCPOFFER has no valid option, the client MUST proceed with a normal DHCPREQUEST. For a DHCPACK that includes the option, a client in the INIT-REBOOT state SHOULD stop DHCPv4 configuration or disable IPv4 for the wait time, and MAY send a DHCPRELEASE. A client in any other state SHOULD keep using its assigned address until the next reconfiguration event. A client that collects several offers MAY use the presence of the option as a selection criterion.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that can live without the old address raises its hand. If the network says 'you can skip it,' the device waits for the stated time. If the network says nothing, it takes an address like always.

sections.title: Server Behavior and RFC 2563
sections.content:
A DHCPv4 server SHOULD be able to configure all or some pools to include the option when a client asks for it, and MAY let operators set a V6ONLY_WAIT timer per pool. It MUST NOT include the option if the pool is not configured as IPv6-mostly, or if the client did not ask for it. If the client did ask and the pool is IPv6-mostly, the server MUST include it.

In that case the server SHOULD NOT assign an address and SHOULD return 0.0.0.0 as the offered address. If that is not feasible, it MAY offer an available pool address, which it SHOULD NOT reserve. If the client then sends a DHCPREQUEST for it, the server MUST process it per RFC 2131. If a client sends both Rapid Commit and the IPv6-Only Preferred option, the server SHOULD NOT honor Rapid Commit when its response would carry the option.

This RFC updates RFC 2563. That RFC says a DHCPDISCOVER without the Auto-Configure option is not answered when no address is chosen. A client that supports only the new option would then get no reply and keep asking. The updated text says such a DISCOVER is not answered only if the IPv6-Only Preferred option is also absent; if it is present, the rules of this RFC apply. To also stop a host from using an IPv4 link-local address, the server sends a yiaddr of 0.0.0.0 with the Auto-Configure flag set to DoNotAutoConfigure.
sections.plainLanguage: On a network that says 'IPv6 is enough,' the helper hands back an empty address slip and a timer. An old rule would have made the helper stay silent, so this document changes that rule.

sections.title: Constants and Transition Assumptions
sections.content:
Two constants govern the wait. V6ONLY_WAIT defaults to 1800 seconds and MUST NOT be less than MIN_V6ONLY_WAIT, which is 300 seconds.

The RFC assumes that the translator in the network is NAT64 (with or without 464XLAT), the only widely supported mechanism at the time of writing. So a server would normally not send the option unless the network provides NAT64. If a different transition technology appeared that needed host support, a new DHCPv4 option would be required. Declaring an interface IPv6-only capable is a policy decision. The RFC gives examples: an OS vendor with 464XLAT enabled, an enterprise that has tested its applications in an IPv6-only environment, or IoT devices that only talk to an IPv6-enabled cloud.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a minimum waiting time so devices do not pester the network, and a normal one if nobody says otherwise. The network should only say 'skip it' if it has a helper that can still reach old-style places.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could send a spoofed DHCPOFFER carrying the option with a huge value such as 0xffffffff, disabling DHCPv4 on supporting clients. On an IPv4-only network those clients would lose connectivity; on a dual-stack network without NAT64, only IPv4-only destinations would be affected. Recovery needs a network attachment event.

The RFC notes that without protection from rogue DHCPv4 servers, a similar attack is possible by offering an invalid address with a Lease Time of 0xffffffff, and that attack hits all hosts. So rogue-server defenses are sufficient here too. The attack also only works if the victim prefers the rogue offer. The RFC adds that turning IPv4 off can be seen as a security feature because it reduces the attack surface.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could tell a device 'wait a very long time.' Guarding against fake helpers on the network already stops that.
